title: New Worlds: We are living in the future of J.G. Ballard or William Gibson
author: speckx
tldr: Ray Newman collects a year of news clippings, from robot dogs and AI soul singers to narco subs and face-recognition glasses, to argue we already live in Ballard's or Gibson's future. What makes it strange is how little anyone notices, because people absorb each new oddity within days and go back to their lives.

keyPoints: Newman borrows Michael Moorcock's habit of opening chapters with newspaper clippings that show the apocalypse already underway, and builds the essay from about twenty real 2025-2026 news excerpts.

The clippings range from an IV drip clinic in a Westfield mall and an AI soul singer with 2.6 million monthly Spotify listeners to a robot that chased boars out of Warsaw and Meta's hidden "NameTag" face recognition for its smart glasses.

The visionaries got the details wrong. Nobody bet on cigarettes or scooters going digital, or on LEDs replacing neon, and the backdrop is wildfires in the English Midlands instead of Blade Runner's acid rain.

The real shock is the lack of shock. His mum asks a voice assistant to remind her about the sprouts, colleagues send AI bots to meetings, and a former colleague's first robotaxi ride got a few weak thumbs-up on LinkedIn.

That leaves science fiction writers stuck, since anything they invent may come true three weeks later and nobody will blink. Newman guesses he would adapt to a world 50 or 100 years ahead in about 48 hours.
article.whyItMatters: Worth reading in full for the clippings themselves, which read like a Ballard collage when stacked together. The summary keeps the argument but loses that cumulative effect.

comments.overview: A lively, mostly agreeing thread that spent its energy on a different question: if this is cyberpunk, why does it feel so drab and so stupid? Commenters argued over whether the future lacks Gibson's style, whether Shenzhen already has it, and whether Gibson was even the right author to name, with long side threads on China, Idiocracy and Ballard reading lists.

themes.title: The dystopia arrived without the style
themes.synthesis: The top thread holds that we got cyberpunk's corporate dystopia with none of its cool, because Amazon and Google look nothing like Arasaka or Hosaka. Others replied that Apple and Disney do have aesthetics people build identities around, that today's look is "Corporate Memphis", and that attempts at sci-fi style give you the Cybertruck and RGB lights. Several readers of Gibson said the cool was never in his corporations anyway. It lived in the subcultures and back alleys, while the commercial mainstream was always meant to be soulless.

quotes.author: keiferski
quotes.text: Which is really the tragedy of it all: we are getting the cyberpunk dystopia with none of the aesthetics that have made it a household word.

quotes.author: saltcured
quotes.text: The scifi backdrop wasn't inherently cool. It was often soulless and dystopian. The crass commercialism and the teeming masses were often depicted as uncool, at least to the narrator's eye.

themes.title: Wrong author: it's Stephenson, Dick, Brunner or Idiocracy
themes.synthesis: Many thought Gibson's dystopias are too competent for the present. The better match is Stephenson's satire, Philip K. Dick's delirium, or Idiocracy's mix of advanced tech and dumb people, and the UFC fight on the White House lawn came up as the clincher. One commenter pushed back hard on Idiocracy, noting its president actually seeks out the smartest man to help his people. Others nominated John Brunner's Stand on Zanzibar and The Shockwave Rider as the most predictive books of all.

quotes.author: krapp
quotes.text: Gibson's dystopias are too competent, too well organized, too *serious.* I feel like we're headed somewhere between the satire of Neal Stephenson and the lunatic delirium of Philip K. Dick.

quotes.author: martythemaniak
quotes.text: In Idiocracy, the nation is led by a person who cares about the well-being of all his constituents and seeks out the most capable person in order to improve the material state of his people.

themes.title: Shenzhen as cyberpunk made real
themes.synthesis: Animats answered the "no aesthetics" complaint with a night walk through Shenzhen: giant screens, synchronized building light shows, drones, robots and self-driving cars. Critics said a well-run, high-tech city has the cyber but none of the punk, with no lowlifes or social collapse in view. It turned into an argument about China's rise, its demographics and whether Gibson, who set his futures in Japan, had predicted Asian dominance all along.

quotes.author: Animats
quotes.text: Shenzhen is cyberpunk made real. Giant display screens everywhere. Light shows on major buildings, synchronized between the buildings.

quotes.author: jmilloy
quotes.text: I see cyber, but where's the punk?  Where's the "lowlife" or the societal collapse?

themes.title: What Gibson got right
themes.synthesis: One commenter credited Gibson with predicting the fusion of governments, corporations, finance, spies and organized crime into amoral "biz", and wondered whether societies have outgrown the scale at which they can hold together. He also said Gibson alone predicted AIs making art, which others rebutted with Vonnegut's EPICAC, Dahl, Orwell's novel machines, Lem and Ballard himself. Fans of the later Jackpot books called them bleaker and closer to where we are, though a few admitted the Sprawl novels are a chore to read.

quotes.author: api
quotes.text: Another thing they got right was the merger of governments, large corporations, finance, intelligence agencies, and globalized organized crime into one big sprawling mass of Machiavellian nihilists scheming for power.

quotes.author: layer8
quotes.text: Once the concept of “electronic brains” was there, the idea that they might also produce art like a human brain can wasn’t far.

themes.title: People who want the dystopia
themes.synthesis: A smaller thread worried about readers who took cyberpunk as a blueprint. Some fans just want neon, dense cities and implants, which need no corporate tyranny. Others picture themselves as the CEO-king of a Night City, and commenters saw that same mindset in Silicon Valley boardrooms.

quotes.author: tancop
quotes.text: Most of them just want neon lights, dense and chaotic cities, space stations, advanced VR, robots and superpowered implants. None of that requires a corporate dystopia, and I think they would make our lives better.

comments.consensus: Most agreed the present has plenty of science-fiction material and that people get used to it fast. Most also agreed it looks drabber and more chaotic than the fiction promised.
comments.dissent: A sizeable group rejected the Gibson framing. They called today messier and more absurd than his well-organized dystopias, and some said the true cyberpunk look already exists in Shenzhen, or that cyberpunk's cool was always confined to its subcultures.

contrarian.author: Terr_
contrarian.text: I think it's worth asking whether "nobody really believes anything" is *itself* the result of a cynical manipulative play, one that occurs in the real world, and thus affects our judgement as we compare "today" versus a sci-fi book.
contrarian.why: While others treated cyberpunk's cynicism as an accurate forecast, Terr_ suggests some regimes manufacture that cynicism on purpose, so accepting it as inevitable plays into their hands.
